title: Advance Athlete Lab Periodization, Taper, and Autoregulation Playbook
license: Owned content — cleared for AI retrieval

chunks.heading: Macro block ratios and recovery weeks
chunks.body: For a typical 12–20 week runway to an A-race, allocate roughly 40% base, 30% build, 20% peak, and 10% taper before the event. Insert a recovery week (roughly 60–70% of prior week's load, no new intensity) every third or fourth build week, or after a B-race mini-block. Short seasons under six weeks compress base and may skip a dedicated peak — never skip taper entirely. Recovery weeks are absorption, not detraining: keep frequency, cut duration and intensity.

chunks.heading: Taper physiology and session selection
chunks.body: Effective tapers reduce volume 40–60% over the final 7–14 days while maintaining short race-pace touches to preserve neuromuscular sharpness. Fitness is largely built; the goal is shedding fatigue without losing feel. Avoid introducing new exercises, big gear changes, or long novel efforts in taper. Sleep, hydration, and carbohydrate availability matter more than squeezing extra quality. If the athlete arrives overreached, a sharper volume cut beats maintaining intensity.

chunks.heading: ACWR sweet spot and limitations
chunks.body: Acute:chronic workload ratio near 0.8–1.3 often reflects sustainable progression when load is measured consistently. Sustained values above ~1.5 suggest a spike relative to recent conditioning; below ~0.8 for multiple weeks may indicate detraining or incomplete return from break. ACWR is a planning signal, not a diagnosis — interpret alongside pain, sleep, HRV trend, and whether the spike was intentional (race week, camp). Do not chase a low ratio with extra load if readiness markers are poor.

chunks.heading: Menstrual cycle and training (non-prescriptive)
chunks.body: Cycle phase may shift perceived effort, sleep, and recovery speed — individual response varies widely. Early follicular days often tolerate standard load; late luteal phase may warrant slightly reduced intensity or shorter intervals if the athlete reports heavy legs, poor sleep, or elevated resting heart rate. Track patterns over several cycles before hard rules. This is autoregulation support, not medical advice; athletes with severe symptoms should consult a clinician. Never prescribe restrictive nutrition or weight targets tied to cycle phase.

chunks.heading: HRV-guided autoregulation
chunks.body: Compare today's HRV and resting heart rate to the athlete's rolling baseline, not population norms. A single suppressed day: downgrade hard sessions to easy aerobic at the same duration. Two or more days suppressed alongside poor sleep or high stress: cut volume ~30% and avoid stacked intensity. When HRV is elevated and the athlete feels good during a build or peak phase, proceed with planned quality — autoregulation also means not holding back when readiness supports the session. Re-test baselines after illness, travel, or large load blocks.

chunks.heading: When to replan a season block
chunks.body: Replan remaining macro phases — not the A-race date — when two or more key sessions are missed in a week, a new B/C race is added mid-season, an active injury requires load reduction, or ACWR stays in the caution zone for consecutive weeks. Preserve the A-race anchor but insert recovery or absorb weeks, then redistribute build and peak time. Communicate the diff clearly: what shifted, why, and what the next two weeks emphasize.

chunks.heading: Base, build, peak defined
chunks.body: Base: aerobic volume, technique, strength foundation, limited intensity. Build: add sport-specific intensity while volume plateaus. Peak: sharpen, trim volume. Then taper. Skipping base to live in build is a common overreaching path.

chunks.heading: Mesocycle length choices
chunks.body: Typical mesocycles run 3–6 weeks including a lighter week. Shorter cycles suit beginners or high-stress life; longer cycles suit advanced athletes with stable recovery. Replan when life or injury breaks the pattern.

chunks.heading: Short vs long taper
chunks.body: Shorter races may use 5–7 day tapers; longer endurance events often use 10–14 days. Cut volume, keep short sharpness, protect sleep and carbs. Over-taper anxiety is normal — coach empathy then trust the plan.

chunks.heading: Functional overreach vs overtraining
chunks.body: Planned overreach with a recovery week can supercompensate. Persistent performance drop, insomnia, mood changes, and illness suggest maladaptation — extend recovery and refer if severe. Do not stack more intensity to 'fix it'.

chunks.heading: Rules after a missed week
chunks.body: Missed most of a week: do not cram seven days into three. Resume with easy frequency, then prior volume, then intensity. Update the calendar honestly.

chunks.heading: Integrating B-races
chunks.body: B-races need mini-tapers and recovery after. Treat them as training stress. Protect A-race by not peaking every month. After a hard B-race, insert absorb days before rebuilding.

chunks.heading: RPE-based autoregulation
chunks.body: If prescribed pace/power feels a full RPE point harder than usual with matched conditions, consider downshifting. RPE works with HRV/sleep — not instead of them when data exists.

chunks.heading: A/B/C goal hierarchy
chunks.body: A-goals drive the season. B-goals support. C-goals are optional fun. When conflicted, protect the A-goal calendar. Say the hierarchy out loud so DIY weeks do not sabotage the race.

chunks.heading: Transition / off-season
chunks.body: After the A-race: reduce structure 1–3 weeks, keep enjoyable movement, address injuries, then rebuild base. Complete sedentary collapse makes return harder — easy play beats total zero for most athletes.

chunks.heading: Weekly anchor sessions
chunks.body: Anchor the week with one long day and at most one to two quality days. Fill the rest with easy and strength/mobility. Anchors make DIY negotiation clearer: protect anchors, trim junk.

chunks.heading: Reverse periodization — when it appears
chunks.body: Some plans emphasize intensity earlier and volume later. It can fit short seasons or experienced athletes. Beginners usually need aerobic base first. Do not flip models mid-block without a reason.

chunks.heading: Block focus weeks
chunks.body: A block may emphasize one quality type (e.g. threshold) for a short stretch, then switch. Keep easy days honest. Do not stack every energy system every week.

chunks.heading: Life stress shares the recovery budget
chunks.body: Work deadlines, exams, and family stress consume recovery. Autoregulate training down when life stress spikes even if the calendar says build. Empathy then a lighter day.
